newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: TENNIS-OPEN REFEREE PUTS EARLY END TO SUMMER.
newsitem.headline: TENNIS-OPEN REFEREE PUTS EARLY END TO SUMMER.

text.p: The sun was shut out of the Australian Open on Tuesday when an official decided to close the Centre Court roof to protect players and public from a heatwave.
But his move was attacked as mid-summer madness.
Tournament referee Peter Bellenger won few friends and plenty of enemies when he decided that Melbourne's famously fickle weather had to be tamed.
Players, coaches and seasoned commentators all complained.
An unrepentant Bellenger, himself nicely bronzed after three days of searing heat and cloudless skies, admitted he of all people would find no comfort in the new indoor conditions.
"Some (players) put the point of view that they trained for these conditions and it gives them an advantage to have the roof open," Bellenger told reporters.
"No matter what decision I make, there will be some that are unhappy and some that will be happy."
It was the understatement of the tournament.
Fourteenth seed Felix Mantilla was furious after falling to Spanish compatriot and friend Carlos Moya in the day's first quarter-final, which was played in still, cool conditions.
"I think it may have been a different match in the sun and the wind," the steamed-up Spaniard said.
On-court temperatures have soared to above 50 degrees Celsius (120 Fahrenheit) over the past two days, turning court surfaces into sticky fly paper and players' legs into lead.

Some players and medical experts warned the conditions could be life-threatening and appealed for tournament officials to lengthen rest breaks. Two top women's players even begged officials to reschedule their match.
Bellenger was unmoved, until Tuesday.
"If it was (fifth seed) Thomas Muster, he wouldn't have even walked out there today," Mantilla fumed.

Mantilla, a fine baseliner, turned out to be a good judge of character. After sweating his way into the quarter-finals with a four set win over Jim Courier on Monday, Muster said the move was unjust, especially for sun-loving fitness fanatics like him.
"If you can't stand the heat and you can't play in these conditions, then you're not a professional," the Austrian hothead told Channel Seven television.
Muster has been known to request his matches be played in the heat of the afternoon.
Second seed Michael Chang is another who likes it hot.
"If you happen to have put in the training and the work so that you can cope with the heat, then you should have the chance to be rewarded," said Chang's brother and coach Carl.
South African Amanda Coetzer, who beat a wilting Steffi Graf on Centre Court at the weekend, said after winning her semifinal berth on Tuesday that she too would have liked the roof open.
"I love playing out in the sun," the untiring blonde said.

But the tournament referee found an ally in Australia's 1960 Wimbledon champion Neale Fraser, now a tennis commentator, who said the stadium roof was designed to protect against all sorts of inclement weather, not just rain.
Even Australia's sports minister, Warwick Smith, waded into the debate, describing the roof's closure as "a victory for common sense".
But U.S. tennis guru Bud Collins was still a little hot under the collar. "The guy stole our summer," he quipped.
"Sir Norman Brookes played under the same sun in 1911 in long flannel trousers and didn't have a seat to sit down on during breaks. Hell -- they didn't even take breaks."
